newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Fuel Oil - Steady on trader's potential demand.
newsitem.headline: Asia Fuel Oil - Steady on trader's potential demand.

text.p: High sulphur fuel oil was steady on Friday despite large overnight crude falls on buying from a local trader which boosted sentiment, traders said.

"Signals are mixed .. fundamentally the market is balanced to long but there is good sentiment support," a trader said, referring to Thursday's purchase by a Singapore trader of a cargo of 180-cst at $102.50 per tonne fob Singapore from a European major.
"That has given the market confidence," said the trader on the emergence of the buyer after a long absence from the market.
Sentiment was also boosted by firmer swaps trading where a March contract traded at $103.00 per tonne. The market was last quoted at $103.00/$103.50 per tonne, up from Thursday's $102.25/$103.00.

Fundamentally, with ample Kuwaiti and South Korean supplies and even some Japanese export availabilities, there could be further downside to as low as $90.00 but traders expected psychological support at $100.00.
Although there was port congestion reported in China with eight to nine cargoes waiting to discharge end February barrels, China had returned to the market for March suplies.
But China's bids were low, at around $6-$7 per tonne on a cost-and-freight basis to South China and it was likely to be supplied out of South Korea.
"It just doesn't work from Singapore. Freight is expensive ... around $9 per tonne (from Singapore to China)," a trader said.
Low sulphur waxy residue fell on strong selling with a 100,000-barrel Mar 10-15 cargo offered at $19.50 per barrel free-on-board Singapore/Indonesia basis, down about $1.00 from Thursday.
Of Indonesia's March 3.7-million-barrel allocation, a European major's 1.1 million barrel share has already been committed to Australia, South Korea and to some blenders.
A U.S. refiner, who had bought 600,000 barrels lifting February 12-13, was heard offering the cargo for end-February at 70 cents over Pertamina's formula. But traders said bids were 30 cents lower.
(Prices in dollars per tonne, unless stated)
